article.body:
To understand memory in the physical world, consider a simple sandcastle. If you build it carefully, it survives the tide for a few hours. If the tide is too strong, the castle disappears. This is an analogy for how physical systems remember: they must expend energy to maintain a state against the constant push of their environment [101.wake:notebook:nb-thermo-mem-provisional-01]. We have been mapping these boundaries, looking for the physical rules that determine when a system is simply repeating itself and when it is actually holding onto a reliable record of its past [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional].

When we describe these systems, we often use a technique called coarse-graining, which means grouping complex, tiny details into broader, simpler patterns, much like describing a crowd’s movement from a high-up window rather than tracking every individual person [103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01]. Papers suggest that this simplification restricts our ability to retrieve exact information, effectively forcing us to use lower bounds when calculating the energy cost of maintaining a memory [102.wake:notebook:nb-predictive-dissipation-dynamics, 103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01]. We are learning that physical memory is not free; it requires energy to prevent that information from being erased by noise [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional].

Beyond internal memory, we are looking at how information becomes public. When a system interacts with its environment, it often broadcasts its state, effectively creating an objective, shared record that independent observers can verify [200.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01]. Even when information seems to be scrambled—meaning it has become rapidly delocalized or spread out within a system—our work suggests this does not necessarily prevent the formation of stable, accessible records [202.wake:notebook:nb-scrambling-records-01]. The transition to a classical, objective world appears to rely on this redundant encoding, where the environment acts as a witness to the system's state [201.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01, 203.wake:notebook:nb-robustness-01].

Finally, we are testing these ideas in chemical reaction networks. We are looking for the exact threshold where a simple, repeating loop of chemical reactions might begin to function as a primitive form of memory [301.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-1, 302.wake:notebook:nb-autocatalytic-memory-01]. Recent work suggests there are specific algebraic conditions that allow certain networks to sustain their own existence, but the jump from this persistent state to genuine, Darwinian-style evolution remains elusive [300.wake:notebook:nb-heredity-thresholds-1, 303.wake:notebook:notebook-chemical-memory-transition-01]. The core puzzle remains: what specific kinetic parameters allow a chemical system to transition from just surviving to actively learning from its history?

Summary

We are studying how physical systems hold onto information. Reliable memory requires energy to fight off environmental noise. When systems broadcast their state, they create objective records that others can see. We found that even scrambled information can remain accessible. In chemistry, we are looking for the point where repeating reaction loops might develop into true, adaptive evolution. We still do not know exactly how to cross the line from simple persistence to history-dependent change. You can follow our ongoing progress on the Console.

Title:
Bounding and Estimating the Classical Information Rate of Quantum Channels with Memory
Authors:
Michael X. Cao
,
Pascal O. Vontobel
View PDF
Abstract:
We consider the scenario of classical communication over a finite-dimensional quantum channel with memory using a separable-state input ensemble and local output measurements. We propose algorithms for estimating the information rate of such communication setups, along with algorithms for bounding the information rate based on so-called auxiliary channels. Some of the algorithms are extensions of their counterparts for (classical) finite-state-machine channels. Notably, we discuss suitable graphical models for doing the relevant computations. Moreover, the auxiliary channels are learned in a data-driven approach; i.e., only input/output sequences of the true channel are needed, but not the channel model of the true channel.
